blocks.heading: Mathematical induction
blocks.text: Mathematical induction proves statements indexed by integers. A starting case and a valid step from each case to the next establish every case in the required range. It is used for sums, powers, and recursive sequences.

blocks.heading: Base case
blocks.text: The base case proves the first required statement directly. If the claim starts at n = 1, prove P(1). If it starts at n = 0 or another integer, use that starting value. The base case cannot be omitted.

blocks.heading: Inductive hypothesis
blocks.text: The inductive hypothesis assumes P(k) for an arbitrary integer k at or above the starting value. This is a temporary assumption used to prove the next case—not an assumption that all cases already hold.

blocks.heading: Inductive step and conclusion
blocks.text: The inductive step uses P(k) to derive P(k + 1). Since k was arbitrary, the implication works at every eligible step. Together with the base case, this proves P(n) for all integers in the stated range.

blocks.heading: Worked example: natural-number sum
blocks.text: Prove 1 + 2 + ⋯ + n = n(n + 1)/2 for n ≥ 1. Base case: when n = 1, both sides are 1. Hypothesis: assume 1 + 2 + ⋯ + k = k(k + 1)/2.

blocks.heading: Natural-number sum: next case
blocks.text:
Using the hypothesis,

1 + 2 + ⋯ + k + (k + 1)
= k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1)
= (k(k + 1) + 2(k + 1))/2
= (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.

This is the formula for k + 1, so induction proves the claim.

blocks.heading: Worked example: odd-number sum
blocks.text: Prove 1 + 3 + ⋯ + (2n − 1) = n² for n ≥ 1. Base case: 1 = 1². Hypothesis: assume the sum of the first k odd numbers is k². Step: add 2k + 1 to obtain k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)². The claim follows by induction.
